artworks.title: Epimetheus and Pandora
artworks.description: Paired wooden sculptures by El Greco of Epimetheus and Pandora as Adam-and-Eve analogues — the afterthought brother and the gifted bride set face to face. The Toledo pair makes Hesiod's marriage visible as a Renaissance meditation on the first human mistake.

artworks.title: Pandora Offers the Jar to Epimetheus
artworks.description: Veronese-school drawing in which Pandora presents the fatal jar to Epimetheus, the brother who accepted Zeus's gift against Prometheus' warning. Farinati freezes the moment before the lid lifts — afterthought already too late.

artworks.title: Epimetheus Opening Pandora's Box
artworks.description: Oil by Anton Tischbein in the Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen (KMS1006): Epimetheus himself pries open Pandora's box while ills pour into the world. The canvas shifts Hesiod's agency onto the husband who looked too late.

artworks.title: Epimetheus Receives Pandora
artworks.description: Outline drawing by John Flaxman for Hesiod's Works and Days: Hermes delivers Pandora to Epimetheus despite Prometheus' warning against gifts from the gods. Neoclassical line turns the brother's acceptance into a cool, fatal handshake.

artworks.title: Prometheus and Epimetheus before Pandora
artworks.description: Academic oil from Berlin's Nationalgalerie: Prometheus and Epimetheus stand before the newly fashioned Pandora, the foresighted brother already uneasy and the afterthought brother already won. Schlösser stages the gift that will undo Epimetheus as a tableau of two temperaments.

popCulture.title: Epimetheus
popCulture.description: Greek epimētheus means afterthought — Prometheus' brother whose name still labels the wisdom that comes too late, after the jar is open.

popCulture.title: Pandora
popCulture.description: Epimetheus' modern afterlife is inseparable from Pandora's — the husband who accepted the gifted bride, and whose failure keeps the jar story alive.
